title: 10 AI Agent Prompts to Improve Your Email Program (Tested by Real Email Teams)
summary: 10 tested AI agent prompts for email teams: audit your block library, turn briefs into drafts, test personalization and QA emails in Dyspatch.
body_markdown:
Since we[launched our MCP server](https://www.dyspatch.io/blog/dyspatch-mcp-server-marketing-ops-meet-your-ai-agent/) , customers keep asking the same thing: "Okay, it's connected. Now what do I ask it?"


Fair question. A blank chat box is a lot of pressure.


So we went through what our services team, our customers and our own marketing team actually ask AI agents to do inside Dyspatch. Then we kept the 10 prompts that saved the most time. Every one comes from a real workflow, and every one is ready to copy, paste and adapt.


The short answer


The best AI agent prompts for email work from your existing templates and blocks, ask for a specific output (a report, a draft, a set of test profiles), and set clear limits (read-only first, don't publish, don't invent IDs). The biggest wins aren't in copywriting. They're in auditing your library, turning briefs into drafts, testing personalization and handing off to developers.


## Before you start: how do I connect an AI agent to Dyspatch?


1. In Dyspatch, open the MCP Server dashboard from the homepage.
2. Find your AI provider and follow its connection instructions or[Launch App link](https://www.dyspatch.io/platform/mcp-agent-operators-in-dyspatch/) .
3. The first time you use it, approve the connection in the pop-up window.
4. Check it worked: ask your agent which Dyspatch user you are, or which workspaces you have.


It works with Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, VS Code with GitHub Copilot and most tools that support MCP. The agent acts as you, with your permissions, so it can't do anything you couldn't already do in Dyspatch. Full details are in the[MCP server documentation](https://docs.dyspatch.io/integrations/mcp-server/) .


One habit for every prompt below: start read-only, look at what it finds, then approve changes.


## Clean up and understand your library


### 1. How healthy is our email account?


Our services team runs this kind of review for customers by hand. One consumer health brand averaging about 97 new emails a month had a beautifully organized library: 50 blocks, none unused. The[guardrail](https://www.dyspatch.io/platform/email-guardrails/) numbers told a different story. 98% of their emails were missing a plain-text version, 62% had a subject or preheader length warning, and 45% had no detectable unsubscribe content. One theme had zero emails in it.


None of that is visible when you're building one email at a time. All of it is visible in one prompt.


```text
Run a read-only health check of my Dyspatch account. Don't change anything.
1. How many emails were created per month over the last 3 months?
2. The 10 most-used blocks and themes, with how many emails use each,
and any blocks or themes no email uses.
3. The share of emails missing plain text, alt text or unsubscribe
content, or with subject or preheader length warnings.
4. Emails exported but never published or approved.
Finish with what we do well, then the top 3 fixes, in priority order.
```


Start with "what we do well." It makes the report much easier to share with your team.


### 2. Which blocks are duplicates, and which one should we keep?


A few years of campaigns leaves near-identical blocks with different names. This prompt finds them by content, not by name, and won't touch anything until you say so.


```text
Review all blocks available through the Dyspatch connection. Find exact
duplicates based on block content and settings, not names.
For each duplicate group, show:
- The blocks and their IDs
- Where each block is used
- Which block you recommend keeping and why
Ask for my approval before making changes. Once approved, update affected
templates to use the kept block. Verify the replacements before removing
any duplicates. If something isn't supported, report it and leave that block alone.
```


### 3. Will our blocks work across all our brands?


One customer runs three brands from one email program. Same blocks, three themes. When we built a demo email and switched it from one brand's theme to another, the section backgrounds stayed in the first brand's mint green. The blocks had colors baked in that the theme couldn't override.


If you run more than one brand, or you're planning a rebrand, check this before it surprises you:


```text
Audit the blocks in our [theme name] theme. Which have hardcoded colors,
fonts or borders that override the theme? Which blocks aren't assigned
to any theme, or only to archived themes? Read-only. Don't change anything.
```


**Tip:** our free[Dyspatch agent skills](https://github.com/getdyspatch/agent-skills) include a block review skill that runs this check with one command.


## Build emails from what you already have


### 4. Can AI turn a project brief into a draft email?


Yes, and our own marketing team does it. Campaign briefs live as tasks in our project management tool. The agent reads the brief, builds the draft in Dyspatch from our approved themes and blocks, posts the link back on the task and moves it to review. A person still reviews every email.


The secret is the workflow section at the bottom of the brief. Steal ours:


```text
Read the brief in [task link]. Create one draft email in Dyspatch,
including subject and preheader. Use existing templates, themes, blocks
and footer. Find the right destination folder; don't invent IDs.
Do not send, schedule, publish or export.
When the draft is created, add the email link and a short summary to the
task, then move it to "Email created: review." Leave it incomplete for
human review. If you get blocked, leave the task where it is and note
the blocker. Never make up an email link.
```


"Never make up an email link" sounds obvious. Write it anyway.


### 5. Can AI build an email from a Figma frame or a Word doc?


Yes. Point the agent at a[Figma frame](https://www.dyspatch.io/platform/figma-to-html-email-export/) , a PDF or Word brief, a screenshot, or even a one-line idea. It builds the email from your existing workspaces, themes, blocks and image library instead of generating new HTML.


```text
Build a new email in Dyspatch from this [Figma frame / attached brief].
Use our [theme name] theme and existing blocks wherever possible.
Add a subject line, preheader and plain-text version, fix any guardrail
warnings, and leave it as an unpublished draft. Tell me which parts
didn't match an existing block.
```


That last line is the useful one. It tells you where your block library has gaps.


### 6. Can AI turn our blog into a newsletter?


Your content team already did the hard part. This prompt does the repackaging, in your newsletter's voice and layout.


```text
Create an unpublished newsletter draft in Dyspatch from the five most
recent posts on our blog. First, review three recent newsletters to learn
our voice, branding and layout, and check our brand guidelines.
Feature the newest post with a larger image, a headline, a 60 to 90 word
summary and a clear CTA. Give the other four 30 to 45 word summaries and
their own links. Use each post's original images with descriptive alt text.
Include a subject line, preheader and plain-text version.
Check that images load and links work. Do not publish or send.
```


When our team ran a version of this, the agent first came back with a detailed proposal. The reply was "yeah that's fine, show me the email." The draft that came back was nearly flawless.


## Test, personalize and hand off


### 7. How do I test every version of a personalized email?


An order confirmation with a first-name fallback, an items loop and conditional rows for discounts, express shipping and tracking can show a customer a dozen different versions. Most teams test two.


Ask the agent to read the email's logic and build one test profile per branch:


```text
Read the variables, loops and conditionals in the [email name] email.
Create one test customer profile for each meaningful version of it,
in a new folder called "[email name] test profiles." Use made-up data,
no real customers. Include an edge case with very long content and one
with every optional field empty. Then preview the email against each
profile and tell me what shows and hides in each.
```


For our test order confirmation, that meant five profiles: a loyalty member with a discount, express shipping with tracking, a guest with no name, a member with express and no discount, and a long-content edge case.


### 8. Can AI write the developer handoff for an email?


One customer built their emails from designs with placeholder content before their data team had decided on field names. Their question for engineering was simple: "Is this what you're expecting?"


```text
Read the [email name] email in Dyspatch and write a handoff brief for
our developers. List every variable, conditional and loop, with the field
name, expected data type, an example value and what it controls.
Separately, list content that looks like it should be personalized but
is hardcoded, marked as "suggested." Include a sample data payload and a
plain-language summary of what the email does. Don't change the email.
```


Your developers get a checklist instead of a scavenger hunt.


### 9. How do I set up an A/B test variant properly?


"Make me a variant" gets you something. Answering a few questions first gets you a test you can learn from. These are the questions our team asks before building one:


- Is this a copy test or a visual test?
- How big is the change? Small (one word in the subject line), medium (the preheader and headline) or large (still realistic for a test)?
- Should the variant be a new draft of this email, or a new email?
- How should the two versions be named and tagged?


```text
Create an A/B variant of the [email name] email. Before you build it, ask
me: copy or visual test, how big the change should be (small, medium or
large), whether to save it as a new draft or a new email, and how to name
and tag both versions. Change only what we agree on.
```


## Review before you ship


### 10. Can AI QA an email right where my team reviews it?


Yes. Instead of exporting HTML into a chat, the agent checks the email in Dyspatch and leaves its findings as comments where your team already reviews.


```text
QA the [email name] email in Dyspatch. Check guardrails, links and
images, spelling for the audience's locale, accessibility, brand,
personalization fallbacks, localizations, subject and preheader, UTMs
and the unsubscribe and legal footer. Rank findings by severity and leave
each one as a comment on the email. Don't apply fixes until I approve them.
```


Our free[agent skills](https://github.com/getdyspatch/agent-skills) include a full QA checklist skill that runs all of this in one go.


## Bonus: three one-liners for Monday morning


```text
Show me all drafts waiting on my approval, with a one-line summary of each.
```


```text
Which of my templates don't have a [French] localization?
```


```text
Which blocks haven't been updated this year?
```


## What makes an agent prompt work?


After a lot of these, here's what we've learned:


- **Start from what already works.** Ask the agent to build from your existing templates and blocks, not from scratch. That's what keeps the output on brand.
- **Say what not to do.** Don't publish, don't send, don't invent IDs, don't change anything yet.
- **Ask for a format.** A ranked list, a table, a handoff brief. Formats are easy to check and easy to share.
- **Name things plainly.** Agents pick blocks by their names and descriptions. "Hero, image left" beats an inside joke every time.
- **Ask it to report what it couldn't do.** The gaps it finds are often the most useful part of the answer.


## Where AI agents still fall short


To be candid about the tradeoffs:


- **The agent acts as you.** That's the point, and also the risk. Start read-only, and keep approval steps in your prompts.
- **Some steps still need a person.** Final export and sending should stay with your email team. We recommend it, and so do our own workflows.
- **Results vary by AI model.** Faster, cheaper models sometimes take shortcuts on complex builds. For multi-step work, use your provider's stronger model.
- **Prompts don't replace a process.** They make a good one faster. They won't fix a missing one.


## Frequently asked questions


What are the best AI prompts for email marketing teams?


The prompts that save the most time go beyond copywriting: an account health check, duplicate block cleanup, brief-to-draft builds, test profiles for personalized emails, developer handoff briefs and QA with comments. Each works from your existing templates and sets clear limits.


What is an MCP server for email?


MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard that lets AI agents connect to other tools. The[Dyspatch MCP server](https://www.dyspatch.io/platform/mcp-agent-operators-in-dyspatch/) lets an agent like Claude or ChatGPT create drafts, review emails,[manage localizations](https://www.dyspatch.io/platform/email-template-localization/) and audit blocks inside your Dyspatch account, with your permissions.


Is it safe to let an AI agent work in our email platform?


The agent can only do what your user role allows, and its actions show up as yours. Some destructive actions, like removing users or API keys, aren't permitted, and edits ask for your approval. Start with read-only prompts.


Do I need a developer to set this up?


No. You connect from the MCP Server dashboard in Dyspatch and approve access. Some company AI setups need an admin to approve a new connector first.


Can AI agents send emails from Dyspatch?


Dyspatch is where you build and approve email, not where you send it. Agents can create drafts and submit them for approval. Sending stays in your ESP, with your team.
